text: The Ray is the name of four superheroes in the DC Comics Universe, all of whom possess the superpower of manipulating visible light in some manner. The first Ray is Langford "Happy" Terrill, a Quality Comics character created by artist Lou Fine, who first appeared in Smash Comics #14 (September 1940) and continued until issue #40 (February 1943). When DC Comics acquired Quality Comics, Happy Terrill was retconned as a member of the Freedom Fighters on Earth-X. Prior to Crisis on Infinite Earths, Happy was exposed to lightning and sunlight simultaneously while ballooning, gaining energy-based powers that allowed him to emit energy and fly. According to Jess Nevins' Encyclopedia of Golden Age Superheroes, The Ray fought Bela Jat, Cadava the Crumbler, Khan the Mongol warrior, and Stradivarius the pied piper of crime. In the Post-Crisis continuity, Happy was part of a secret government group called RONOL, where Dr. Dayzl theorized that a light entity from the early universe would return as a conscious, dangerous force. To stop it, Dayzl tricked Happy into a ballooning "accident" that exposed him to a genetic "light bomb," intending for his offspring to become a human-light energy union capable of communicating with the entity. Unaware of the truth, Happy became the Ray. RONOL lost government support due to Dayzl’s unorthodox theories, and Dayzl’s fate remains unknown. In February 1946, Happy and his first wife, Gayle, had a son named Joshua, who accompanied him as a sidekick named Spitfire. Joshua exhibited violent outbursts and, on his birthday in February 1954, accidentally killed his mother; he was then placed in suspended animation and later awakened in the future, still only 8 years old. After a brief return to the Freedom Fighters in the 1970s, Happy married Nadine and settled down. In 1950, after learning the truth, he vowed to retire from the Ray identity. When his newborn son Raymond glowed with energy in the hospital, Happy believed Dayzl’s theories were correct and, to protect his wife, told her the baby had died and placed Raymond with his brother Thomas as a foster child. In the 2008 Freedom Fighters series, Happy was asked by Uncle Sam to seek help from Neon the Unknown, who refused; Happy then drank from Neon’s oasis and became a new version of Neon, known simply as "Neon." Ray Terrill, raised in darkness due to a false belief that he was hypersensitive to light, wished for normalcy and had only one friend, neighbor Jennifer Jurden. At 18, during his supposed father’s deathbed, Ray discovered his life was a lie—he was not allergic to light and did not need to live in darkness, and his true father was the Golden Age Ray. A later version of the Ray is Stan Silver, who, while working as a foreign correspondent for the Washington Sun, was exposed to upper atmosphere radiation and gained powers allowing him to turn his body into a living laser light. Described by Justin Gray as "the playboy of the group," Silver is a womanizing egomaniac in civilian life. Recruited by S.H.A.D.E., he later defects to join Uncle Sam’s Freedom Fighters. In Uncle Sam and the Freedom Fighters #6, Silver reveals he is a double agent loyal to S.H.A.D.E., turns on his teammates, kills the Invisible Hood, and his costume inverts from yellow to blue. In #7, he battles his former teammates, is defeated by Ray Terrill, and is sent back to Father Time, later seen outside the White House with S.H.A.D.E. soldiers who join Father Time in the timestream. In 2011’s New 52 relaunch, Lucien Gates, a Korean-American San Diego County lifeguard, was introduced as the Ray in a miniseries titled The Ray, written by Palmiotti and Gray with art by Jamal Igle, which debuted in December 2011 and did not feature prior incarnations. Gates was caught in a particle beam accidentally fired from a solar energy cannon by an unnamed government agency, which mutated him into an energy manipulator capable of flying at superhuman speed, firing energy beams, creating illusions, and manipulating light. Unlike other versions, Gates cannot become immaterial; instead, light forms a protective armor. He travels in a straight line and must strike a reflective surface to change direction, though he can redirect at any angle, similar to a swimmer kicking off a pool edge. He can reduce speed and hover. All versions of the Ray can absorb, store, and process pure light to fly and create powerful bursts of light. Happy Terrill could also manipulate electricity and magnetism and create illusions, solid light constructs, and render himself invisible. Later, Happy demonstrated greater mastery, using "solid light vibrations" to simulate telepathic communication. Ray Terrill can convert his entire body into light energy, making him invulnerable in that form. Stan Silver’s full powers are largely undocumented, with only his ability to turn into a living laser light being noted. Lucien Gates’ thought processes calculate hundreds of options, allowing him to redirect his path at light speed. Kurt Mitchell, in American Comic Book Chronicles: 1940–1944, notes that the Golden Age strip showcased Lou Fine’s mastery of lighting effects and wild fight scenes with memorable, ugly villains. The Ray Terrill incarnation appears in the Arrowverse crossover "Crisis on Earth-X," the CW Seed animated series Freedom Fighters: The Ray, and in an uncredited appearance in "Crisis on Infinite Earths," portrayed by Russell Tovey. An unidentified Ray also appears in Justice League: Crisis on Infinite Earths - Part One.
